body: Liechtenstein licence plates are black with white letters and have a yellow-and-red emblem on the left. The plates look grey when blurred, but the emblem's colors are still visible.
Liechtenstein is mostly a flat river valley with tall mountains visible in nearly every direction, especially to the east. The landscape is dominated by pastures and agricultural land.
All coverage in Liechtenstein uses a low-cam setup, resulting in a larger car blur and a lower viewing angle. This is a key feature shared only with Switzerland and Japan.
Liechtenstein uses black-and-white cylindrical bollards with a rounded top and often a blue side attachment. These are nearly identical to some bollards found in Switzerland.
Bus stops feature a green-and-white sign with the word 'LIEMOBIL' at the top, often framed by a black metallic border.
Directional signs are similar to Switzerland, being white for smaller roads and blue for larger roads. They feature a pointed arrowhead in a contrasting color.
Pedestrian signs have a unique combination of seven stripes and a tall rectangular shape. These signs are identical to those in Switzerland.
Road separators are striped yellow-and-black with a rounded top and a 'Lego-like' knob. These can be identical to some separators in Switzerland.
Road signs in Liechtenstein often have a round, grey metal border. This feature can also be seen in Switzerland and Germany.
The architecture is a mix of traditional Alpine styles and modern buildings, particularly in larger cities.
The Triesenberg area is a populated region on the eastern mountain slope, overlooking the Rhine Valley to the west.
The area east of the main mountain ridge is surrounded by mountains on all sides.
The Ruggell area is characterized by a small, forested ridgeline to the south, which is less imposing than the mountains in the rest of the country.
The Mauren area is urban and lies south of a small ridge, with large mountains visible to the south and southeast.
A unique landscape of rolling hills stretches from Bendern northeast to the Austrian border, contrasting with the country's otherwise flat or mountainous terrain.
In the flat area west of Balzers, with its gridded roads, you can often spot two rocky peaks in Switzerland to the northwest.
Vaduz is unique for sometimes using red bus stop signs, in addition to the standard green and white ones.
Balzers can be identified by its occasional use of black bus stop signs.
Blue street signs with a thin white border are found in the south of the country or near Bendern in the north.
Blue street signs with no outline are specific to the town of Eschen.
Simple, flat black street signs are characteristic of eastern Liechtenstein.
Schaan features distinctive black street signs with a white border and embossed letters.
Brown street signs with a traditional German-style font and a white border are found in Vaduz and the northern towns.
Arrow-shaped brown street signs are a unique feature of Ruggell.
Brown street signs with a more 'generic' font are used in Planken.
A steep, rocky cliff with trees at its base and top is a landmark in and around Mäls.
The only lakes in the country are located in the mountains, just south of Steg.
